inline.s: Appearances are manifested therein, yet in truth nothing exists.
So too it is with consciousness: it manifests all forms universally;
Like a flame in a dream, like a barren woman’s child.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the teachings of the Buddhas transcend the four propositions — that is, they are free from the propositions of unity and difference, of both and of neither, and of being and non-being, and from the assertions and denials built upon them. Mahāmati, the teachings of the Buddhas have as their foremost principles the truths, dependent origination, cessation, the path, and liberation; they are not in accord with such notions as a primal cause, a sovereign lord, a personal creator, fate, time, or atoms. Mahāmati, the teachings of the Buddhas are spoken to purify the two obstructions, those of affliction and of cognition; by stages they establish beings in the one hundred and eight unmarked dharmas, and yet they skillfully distinguish the marks of the various vehicles and stages, like a caravan leader who skillfully guides a company.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are: the dhyāna practiced by the unenlightened, the dhyāna investigating meaning, the dhyāna resting on suchness, and the dhyāna of the Tathāgatas. Mahāmati, what is the dhyāna practiced by the unenlightened? It is that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, knowing the non-existence of a personal self, see that their own and others’ bodies are but chains of bones linked together, all marked by impermanence, suffering, and impurity. Contemplating in this way and clinging to it without letting go, they advance stage by stage until they reach the absorption of the extinction of perception and feeling; this is called the dhyāna practiced by the unenlightened. What is the dhyāna investigating meaning? It is to know that the self-nature and the shared nature of a personal self do not exist, to be free of the sectarian views that things are made by oneself, by another, or by both, and to contemplate in accordance with the meaning of the stages of the non-existence of a self in dharmas; this is called the dhyāna investigating meaning. What is the dhyāna resting on suchness? It is that when one discriminates the non-existence of a self one falls into the two notions of existence and non-existence, which are false thoughts; but when one knows things as they truly are, those thoughts do not arise; this is called the dhyāna resting on suchness. What is the dhyāna of the Tathāgatas? It is to enter the ground of the Buddhas and dwell in the threefold joy of the noble wisdom that is realized within oneself, and to perform inconceivable deeds for the sake of all beings; this is called the dhyāna of the Tathāgatas.”
“The dhyāna of the unenlightened, the dhyāna that contemplates meaning’s marks,
The dhyāna resting on suchness, the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna.
The practitioner in absorption beholds the shapes of sun and moon,
The perilous depths of lotuses, the void, fire, and painted forms;
On such marks as these he dwells and falls into the sectarian dharmas;
He falls as well into the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha realms.
Renouncing all of this, he dwells where there is no object;
Then he can enter in accord with the true mark of suchness.
In the lands of the ten directions, all the countless Buddhas;
All extend their luminous hands and stroke the crown of that one’s head.”
Then Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as for the nirvāṇa spoken of by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, what dharma is it that is called nirvāṇa?”

The Buddha told Mahāmati: “When the habit-energies of the self-nature of all consciousness, and the habit-energies of the storehouse consciousness, the manas, and the mental consciousness, have been transformed, I and all the Buddhas call this nirvāṇa; that is, the realm in which the nature of all dharmas is emptiness. Moreover, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is the realm traversed by the noble wisdom that is realized within oneself, far removed from annihilation and permanence and from being and non-being. Why is it not permanent? Because it is free from all discriminations of self-nature and shared nature. Why is it not annihilated? Because it is the realm traversed by the self-realized wisdom of all the noble ones of past, future, and present. Moreover, Mahāmati, the great nirvāṇa is indestructible and deathless. If it died, one would have to undergo birth again; if it were destroyed, it would be conditioned. Therefore nirvāṇa is indestructible and deathless, and it is the refuge toward which all practitioners tend. Moreover, Mahāmati, because there is nothing abandoned and nothing attained, because it is neither annihilated nor permanent, and because it is neither one nor different, it is called nirvāṇa. Moreover, Mahāmati, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, knowing self-nature and shared nature, forsake the tumult of the world, do not give rise to inversions, and do not give rise to discrimination; it is in this that they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of marks of self-nature. What are the two? They are: the mark of self-nature that clings to words, and the mark of self-nature that clings to dharmas. The mark of self-nature that clings to words arises from the habit-energy of clinging to words through beginningless conceptual elaboration. The mark of self-nature that clings to dharmas arises from not awakening to what is manifested by one’s own mind.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of empowerment of the Buddhas, by which the bodhisattvas are sustained and made to bow at the feet of the Buddhas and inquire into the manifold meanings. What are the two? They are: causing them to enter samādhi, and manifesting a body before them to anoint their crowns with the hand. Mahāmati, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas on the first ground, sustained by the power of the Buddhas, enter the great-vehicle light samādhi of the bodhisattvas; having entered it, all the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before them and empower them in body and speech, as in the case of Vajragarbha and the other bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have accomplished such marks of merit. Mahāmati, when this bodhisattva mahāsattva, sustained by the Buddhas’ power, has entered samādhi, he gathers all roots of goodness throughout a hundred thousand kalpas, gradually enters the several grounds, skillfully comprehends the marks of what is to be remedied and what remedied it, and arrives at the ground of the Dharma-cloud, in a subtle and wondrous palace of great lotuses, seated upon a jewel throne, surrounded by bodhisattvas of his own kind, wearing a jeweled crown, his body like gold, his color like the campaka flower, like the full moon, pouring forth great radiance; and the Buddhas of the ten directions extend lotus hands and anoint his crown upon that throne. Just as the crown prince of a wheel-turning king, having received anointment, attains sovereign mastery, so too are these bodhisattvas. This is called the two. Because the bodhisattva mahāsattvas are sustained by these two kinds of empowerment, they can personally see all the Buddhas; otherwise they cannot. Moreover, Mahāmati, when the bodhisattva mahāsattvas enter samādhi and manifest transcendent powers and teach the Dharma, all of this comes about through the two kinds of empowerment of the Buddhas. Mahāmati, if bodhisattvas could teach the Dharma apart from the Buddhas’ empowerment, then ordinary beings too should be able to teach. Mahāmati, in mountains and forests, among grasses and trees, in walled cities and palaces, and in all musical instruments, wherever the Tathāgata arrives, by the Buddhas’ sustaining power the sound of the Dharma is proclaimed; how much more so for those who have mind — the deaf, the blind, and the mute are freed from suffering and liberated. Mahāmati, the sustaining power of the Tathāgata has such vast and mighty effects.”

Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha: “Why does the Tathāgata, by his sustaining power, cause the bodhisattvas to enter samādhi and to receive, on a surpassing ground, the anointing of his hand upon their crowns?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is in order to cause them to be far removed from the deeds of Māra and all afflictions, in order that they may not fall to the ground of the śrāvakas, in order that they may quickly enter the Tathāgata’s ground, and in order that the dharmas they have attained may increase doubly, that the Buddhas sustain the bodhisattvas by the power of their empowerment. Mahāmati, were it not so, those bodhisattvas would fall into the midst of the sectarian and śrāvaka-Māra realms, and would not be able to attain unsurpassed bodhi; therefore the Tathāgata embraces the bodhisattvas by the power of his empowerment.”
“The World-Honored One’s pure vow has a great sustaining power;
From the first ground to the tenth, in samādhi and in consecration.”

Then Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, the Buddha teaches dependent origination as arising from a maker, not as arising from itself. The sectarians also say that a sovereign lord, a personal creator, time, a self, and atoms give rise to all dharmas. Now the World-Honored One merely uses a different name and calls it dependent origination, but the meaning is no different. World-Honored One, the sectarians also say that through an agent, being arises from non-being; the World-Honored One also says that through causes and conditions all dharmas, originally non-existent, arise, and having arisen return to cessation. As the Buddha says, ‘conditioned by ignorance, the formations, and so on, down to old age and death’ — this is to teach no-cause, not to teach a cause. The World-Honored One says that when this exists, that exists; but if both are established at one and the same time and not in a sequence of mutual dependence, the meaning cannot stand. Therefore the sectarians speak well, and not the Tathāgata. And why? The sectarians say that a cause not born from conditions yet produces what is produced; but what the World-Honored One teaches is that the fruit waits upon the cause and the cause again waits upon a cause, and so on without end, which is the fault of infinite regress. Moreover, if when this exists that exists, then there is no cause at all.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, I understand that all dharmas are what is manifested by mind alone, with no grasper and no grasped; and it is thus that I say, ‘when this exists, that exists,’ not the fault of no-cause, nor the fault of causes and conditions. Mahāmati, if one does not understand that all dharmas are what is manifested by mind alone, one conceives of a grasper and a grasped, clings to outer objects as existing or not existing, and it is that one who has this fault, not I who speak thus.”
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, because there is speech, there must be dharmas; if there were no dharmas, on what would speech depend for its arising?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, even where there are no dharmas there is still speech. Do we not plainly see that people speak of such things as turtle hair, rabbit horns, and a barren woman’s child? Mahāmati, these are neither existent nor non-existent, and yet there is speech about them. Mahāmati, if, as you say, dharmas exist because there is speech about them, that argument is ruined. Mahāmati, not all Buddha lands have speech; speech is merely a provisional designation. Mahāmati, in some Buddha lands the Dharma is revealed by gazing, in others by the manifestation of strange marks, or again by the raising of the eyebrows, or by the movement of the eyes, or by a smile, a frown, a groan, a cough, a recollection, a stirring — by such means as these the Dharma is revealed. Mahāmati, in such worlds as the World of No Winking, the World of Wondrous Fragrance, and the Buddha land of Samantabhadra Tathāgata, by gazing alone without winking the bodhisattvas are made to attain the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and all the surpassing samādhis. Mahāmati, it is not because of speech that dharmas exist; in this world, such creatures as flies and ants accomplish their own affairs without speech.”
“Like a hare’s horn in the void, and like a barren woman’s child;
Non-existent, and yet there is speech of them — so the foolish conceive of dharmas.
In the meeting of causes and conditions, the foolish vainly say there is birth;
Unable to understand things as they are, they wander through the three realms of existence.”
Then Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, that which is spoken of as the abiding sound — on what does it depend that you speak of it?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is spoken with reliance on the deluded dharmas; for the deluded dharmas are manifested even to the noble ones, and yet they are not inverted. Mahāmati, just as with a mirage, a wheel of fire, falling hairs, a gandharva city, a dream, an illusion, and a mirror image, the unwise in the world give rise to inverted understanding, while the wise do not; and yet these things are not unmanifested. Mahāmati, when the deluded dharmas are manifested there are countless differences, and yet they are not impermanent. And why? Because they are beyond being and non-being. How are they beyond being and non-being? Because of the various understandings of all the foolish: as with the water of the Ganges, some see it and some do not; the hungry ghosts do not see it, so it cannot be called existent, and since others see it, it cannot be called non-existent. The noble ones are free from inverted views regarding the deluded dharmas. Mahāmati, the deluded dharmas are constant, because their marks do not differ; it is not that the deluded dharmas have differing marks, but that through discrimination there comes to be difference. Therefore the essence of the deluded dharmas is constant. Mahāmati, how does one attain the reality of the deluded dharmas? It is that the noble ones do not give rise to inversion regarding the deluded dharmas, and do not have inverted perception; if one has the least notion regarding the deluded dharmas, that is not noble wisdom; one who has the least notion should be known to be engaged in the conceptual elaboration of the foolish, not in the speech of the noble.

“Mahāmati, if one discriminates the deluded dharmas as inverted or not inverted, one then accomplishes two kinds of lineage, namely: the noble lineage and the ordinary lineage. Mahāmati, the noble lineage is again of three kinds: the śrāvaka, the pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha vehicle, because they differ. Mahāmati, how is it that the foolish, discriminating the deluded dharmas, give rise to the lineage of the śrāvaka vehicle? By clinging to self-nature and shared nature. Mahāmati, how is it that the foolish, discriminating the deluded dharmas, accomplish the lineage of the pratyekabuddha vehicle? By clinging to self-nature and shared nature while free from the tumult of the world. Mahāmati, how is it that the wise, discriminating the deluded dharmas, accomplish the lineage of the Buddha vehicle? By comprehending that all is nothing but what is seen through the discrimination of one’s own mind, with no external dharmas. Mahāmati, when the foolish discriminate the various things of the deluded dharmas as definitely so and definitely not otherwise, this accomplishes the lineage of birth and death. Mahāmati, the various things within those deluded dharmas are neither things nor non-things. Mahāmati, it is in regard to those very deluded dharmas that the noble and wise ones, because the evil habit-energies of mind, manas, and consciousness and the dharmas of self-nature have been turned about, call this delusion suchness; and therefore suchness is beyond mind and consciousness. I now clearly reveal this teaching: those who are free from discrimination are free from all discriminations.”
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said: “World-Honored One, the deluded dharmas you speak of — are they existent or non-existent?”

The Buddha said: “They are like an illusion, because they have no mark of grasping. If the mark grasped were real, it could not be transformed, and then dependent origination would be as the sectarians say, produced by an agent.”
Mahāmati said again: “If the deluded dharmas are the same as an illusion, then they should become the cause of other delusions.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, illusory things are not the cause of delusion and confusion, because illusions do not give rise to any fault, and because illusory things are without discrimination. Mahāmati, illusory things arise from the mantras of others, not from the power of the habitual faults of one’s own discrimination; therefore illusory things do not give rise to fault. Mahāmati, these dharmas of delusion and confusion are grasped only by the minds of the foolish, not by the noble ones.”
“The noble ones do not see the deluded dharmas, nor is what lies between them real;
Because delusion itself is truth, what lies between them is real as well.
If, apart from the deluded dharmas, there were a mark that arises;
This would again be delusion, as when a cataract is not yet cleared.
“Moreover, Mahāmati, because the dharmas are seen to be not illusory and to have nothing resembling them, it is said that all dharmas are like an illusion.”

Mahāmati said: “World-Honored One, is it with reliance on clinging to various illusory marks that you say all dharmas are like an illusion? Or is it with reliance on something else, on this clinging and inverted mark? If it is with reliance on clinging to various illusory marks that you say all dharmas are like an illusion, World-Honored One, then not all dharmas are like an illusion. And why? Because the seeing of various forms does not come about without a cause. World-Honored One, there is no cause at all that makes the various forms appear like an illusion. Therefore, World-Honored One, it cannot be said that with reliance on clinging to various illusory marks, all dharmas resemble an illusion.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, it is not with reliance on clinging to various illusory marks that I say all dharmas are like an illusion. Mahāmati, because all dharmas are unreal and swiftly perish like lightning, I say they are like an illusion. Mahāmati, just as a flash of lightning is seen and at once ceases, so all the foolish and unenlightened of the world plainly see all dharmas manifested by self-nature and shared nature through their own discrimination; and because they cannot observe that nothing exists, they vainly conceive and cling to various forms.”
“Not illusory, without resemblance, and no dharmas either;
Unreal and swift as lightning — one should know them as an illusion.”

Then Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha said before, all dharmas are entirely without arising; and you also say they are like an illusion. Is this not a contradiction between what was said before and what is said after?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, there is no contradiction. And why? Because I understand that arising itself is non-arising, since it is nothing but what is seen by one’s own mind. Whether existent or non-existent, all external dharmas are seen to be without nature and primordially unarisen. Mahāmati, in order to free beings from the sectarian doctrine of arising from a cause, I say that all dharmas are altogether unarisen. Mahāmati, the sectarians gather in crowds and raise evil views together, saying that all dharmas arise from being or from non-being, not that they arise from the condition of their own clinging and discrimination. Mahāmati, I say that all dharmas are not born from being or non-being; therefore they are called unarisen. Mahāmati, those who teach the dharmas do so in order to make disciples understand that they are bound to birth and death by their various actions, and to block their view of annihilation. Mahāmati, those who teach that the marks of all dharmas are like an illusion do so in order to free beings from the marks of the self-nature of dharmas. Because the foolish and unenlightened fall into evil views and desires, not knowing that all dharmas are what is manifested by mind alone, and in order to make them turn away from clinging to the marks produced by causes and conditions, I teach that all dharmas are like an illusion and a dream. Those foolish ones, clinging to evil views, deceive themselves and others, and cannot clearly see the true abiding place of all dharmas. Mahāmati, to see the true abiding place of all dharmas is to comprehend that they are what is manifested by mind alone.”
“Because there is no making, there is no arising; dharmas exist and embrace birth and death;
Comprehending them as like an illusion and the rest, one does not discriminate their marks.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, I shall now teach the marks of name, sentence, and letter. If the bodhisattva mahāsattvas skillfully observe these marks and comprehend their meaning, they will quickly attain anuttarā-samyak-saṁbodhi, and will also be able to awaken all beings. Mahāmati, as for the name-body: it is that a name is established in dependence on a thing, and the name itself is the body; this is called the name-body. As for the sentence-body: it is that it can reveal the meaning decisively and conclusively; this is called the sentence-body. As for the letter-body: it is that by means of these one can accomplish names and sentences; this is called the letter-body. Moreover, Mahāmati, the sentence-body is the conclusive grasp of the matter of a sentence. The name-body is the various letters and names, each one distinct, as from the letter a up to the letter ha. The letter-body is long and short, high and low. Moreover, the sentence-body is like a footprint, like the tracks of men and beasts in a street or lane. A name is the four immaterial aggregates, because it is spoken by name. A letter is the self-mark of the name, because it is manifested by the letter. These are called the name-body, the sentence-body, and the letter-body. These marks of name, sentence, and letter you should cultivate and learn.”
“The name-body and the sentence-body, and the letter-body’s distinctions;
These the foolish and unenlightened cling to, like an elephant sunk in deep mud.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, in future ages there will be those of perverse wisdom and evil thought who, departing from the Dharma as it is, will look upon the marks of unity and difference, of both and of neither, and will question the wise. They will be answered: this is not a proper question. Namely: are form and impermanence different, or not different? And likewise nirvāṇa and the formations, the characterized and the characterizing, the basis and what is based upon it, the maker and what is made, the seer and what is seen, earth and atoms, wisdom and the wise — are they different or not different? Questioned thus in due order about the unanswerable matters, the World-Honored One said that these should be set aside and not answered. The unwise and foolish are not able to know them, and the Buddha, wishing to make them free from the ground of fear, does not answer them. Mahāmati, the reason for not answering is to cause the sectarians to attain final deliverance from the view of a maker. Mahāmati, the sectarians reckon a maker and speak thus: ‘the life-force is the body, or the life-force is different and the body is different.’ Statements such as these are called the unanswerable teachings. Mahāmati, it is the deluded sectarians who speak the unanswerable teachings; it is not that in my teaching, which is free from grasper and grasped and does not give rise to discrimination, anything is to be set aside. Mahāmati, if one clings to a grasper and a grasped, not understanding that it is nothing but what is seen by one’s own mind, that one should be set aside. Mahāmati, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach the Dharma to beings by four kinds of exposition. Mahāmati, the teaching that is to be set aside I spoke at another time, because the faculties of beings were not yet mature, and so for the time being it was set aside.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, why are all dharmas unarisen? Because they are free from maker, made, and agent. Why do all dharmas have no self-nature? Because, when observed by the wisdom of realization, self-nature and shared nature are unattainable. Why do all dharmas neither come nor go? Because, as to self-nature and shared nature, they come from nowhere and go nowhere. Why are all dharmas not annihilated? Because all dharmas are without nature and mark, and are unattainable. Why are all dharmas impermanent? Because all marks arise and are of the nature of impermanence. Why are all dharmas permanent? Because the arising of marks is itself non-arising, since nothing exists. The nature of impermanence is itself permanent; therefore I say that all dharmas are permanent.”
“Direct and counter-questioning, analytical and setting aside;
By these four kinds of exposition, all the sectarians are overthrown.
The Sāṃkhya and the Vaiśeṣika speak of birth from being and non-being;
All such teachings as these are altogether unanswerable.
When observed by wisdom, their essence is unattainable;
Since it cannot be spoken, it is called without self-nature.”

Then Mahāmati Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha: “World-Honored One, may you explain to me the marks of the stages and fruits of the śrāvakas — of the stream-enterer, and of the fruit of stream-entry — so that I and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas, hearing this meaning, may become skilled in the marks of the skillful means relating to the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat. And so may we expound it for beings, causing them to realize the twofold selflessness, to purify the two obstructions, to penetrate the marks of the stages in due order, and to attain the Tathāgata’s inconceivable realm of wisdom, like a mani jewel of many colors, bringing benefit to all beings.”
The Buddha said: “Listen well, and I shall tell you.”
Mahāmati said: “Indeed.”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, the stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry have three grades of difference: lower, middling, and higher. Mahāmati, the lower is reborn at most seven times among the realms of existence; the middling, in three or five births; the higher enters nirvāṇa in this very life. Mahāmati, these three kinds of persons cut off three fetters: the view of a body, doubt, and the clinging to rites and vows; and advancing higher and higher, they attain the fruit of the arhat. Mahāmati, the view of a body is of two kinds: the innate and the discriminated, as, relying on dependent origination, there is an imagined nature. Mahāmati, just as, relying on the nature of dependent origination, various imagined and clinging natures arise, so those dharmas are merely marks of false discrimination, neither existent nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent; yet the foolish and deluded ordinary beings cling to them perversely, like a thirsty beast that falsely gives rise to the notion of water. This discriminated view of a body, because of lack of wisdom, accords with one for a long time, but when one sees the selflessness of persons it is at once abandoned. Mahāmati, as for the innate view of a body: by comprehensively observing one’s own and others’ bodies, one sees that the four aggregates beginning with feeling are without form or mark, that form arises from the great elements, that the great elements are mutually causal, and that form is not accumulated; having observed thus, one clearly sees existence and non-existence and at once abandons it. Because the view of a body is abandoned, greed does not arise; this is the mark of the view of a body. Mahāmati, as for the mark of doubt: because one rightly sees the mark of the dharmas realized, and because the two kinds of view of a body have been discriminated and cut off, doubt cannot arise regarding any dharma, nor does one form the notion of a great teacher as pure or impure in regard to others; this is the mark of doubt. Mahāmati, why does the stream-enterer not adopt rites and vows? Because he clearly sees the marks of suffering in the places of rebirth, he does not adopt them. As for those who do adopt them, they are the foolish and unenlightened who, amid the realms of existence, crave worldly pleasures and practice austerities and observe precepts in the wish to be born there. The stream-enterer does not adopt these marks, but seeks only the supreme, undefiled, undiscriminating dharma that is to be realized, and cultivates the aggregate of precepts; this is the mark of clinging to rites and vows. Mahāmati, because the stream-enterer abandons the three fetters, he is free from greed, hatred, and delusion.”
Mahāmati said: “Greed is of many kinds; which greed is abandoned?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, he abandons the tangling craving and desire for the forms of women, because he sees that the pleasure now present gives rise to future suffering, and because he attains the surpassing joy of samādhi; therefore he abandons that, but not the craving for nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, what is the fruit of the once-returner? It is that, not comprehending the marks of form, he gives rise to discrimination regarding form; having returned once more, he well cultivates the practices of dhyāna, reaches the end of suffering, and enters parinirvāṇa; this is called the once-returner. Mahāmati, what is the fruit of the non-returner? It is that, in regard to the marks of form past, future, and present, he gives rise to views of existence and non-existence, but the discriminations and latent faults no longer arise; he abandons all fetters forever and never returns again; this is called the non-returner. Mahāmati, as for the arhat: he has accomplished all dhyānas, samādhis, liberations, powers, and transcendent faculties; the afflictions, sufferings, and discriminations are forever exhausted; this is called the arhat.”

Mahāmati said: “World-Honored One, there are three kinds of arhat: those who incline wholly to cessation, those who have retreated from the bodhisattva vow, and those who are emanations of the Buddha. Which of these do you mean?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, I mean those who incline to cessation, not the others. Mahāmati, the other two kinds are those who have already made vows of skillful means, and those who manifest birth there in order to adorn the assemblies of the Buddhas. Mahāmati, in the midst of delusion various dharmas are taught; for the realized fruit, the meditator, and the dhyāna are all by nature apart, and the marks of the fruit are what is seen by one’s own mind. Mahāmati, if the stream-enterer should think, ‘I am free from the fetters,’ he would have two faults: he would fall into the view of a self, and the fetters would not be cut off. Moreover, Mahāmati, one who wishes to pass beyond all dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless realms should be free from the marks seen by his own mind. Mahāmati, that the samādhi of the extinction of perception and feeling should transcend the sphere seen by one’s own mind is not so, because it is not apart from mind.”
“The dhyānas and the immeasurables, the formless samādhis,
And the extinction of perception and feeling: in mind alone they are unattainable.
The stream-enterer and the once-returner, the non-returner, the arhat;
All such noble ones as these are established wholly in the deluded mind.
The dhyāna, the meditator, and the object of dhyāna, the cutting off of affliction and the seeing of the truth;
All these are false imagining; knowing this, one is at once liberated.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of wisdom of awakening: the wisdom of observation, and the wisdom of grasping marks, discriminating, and establishing. The wisdom of observation is to observe that all dharmas, being beyond the four propositions, are unattainable. The four propositions are: unity and difference, both and neither, being and non-being, permanence and impermanence, and the rest. Because all dharmas are beyond these four propositions, I say that all dharmas are beyond. Mahāmati, you should cultivate and learn this way of observing. What is the wisdom of grasping marks, discriminating, and establishing? It is to grasp at the marks of the natures of the great elements, solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion, and to discriminate them falsely, and to establish them falsely by means of thesis, reason, and example; this is called the wisdom of grasping marks, discriminating, and establishing. These are called the two kinds of mark of the wisdom of awakening. When the bodhisattva mahāsattva knows these marks of wisdom, he can comprehend the selflessness of persons and dharmas, and by the wisdom without marks he skillfully observes on the ground of understanding and practice, enters the first ground and gains a hundred samādhis, and by the power of that surpassing samādhi sees a hundred Buddhas and a hundred bodhisattvas, knows the affairs of a hundred kalpas in the periods before and after, illumines a hundred Buddha worlds, and skillfully comprehends the marks of the higher and higher grounds; by the power of his surpassing vows he manifests transformations at will, and arriving at the ground of the Dharma-cloud he receives consecration, enters the Buddha-ground, and by his ten inexhaustible vows brings beings to accomplishment, appearing in various responsive forms without rest, while ever dwelling in the surpassing joy of the samādhi of the realm of self-realization.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should skillfully understand the great elements and the forms they produce. How should he understand them? Mahāmati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should observe thus: those great elements are in truth unarisen, because the three realms are nothing but discrimination, manifested by mind alone with no external things. When he observes thus, the forms produced by the great elements are all apart by nature, beyond the four propositions, free from self and what belongs to self, and he dwells in the abode of reality and accomplishes the mark of non-arising. Mahāmati, how do those great elements produce forms? Mahāmati, it is by false discrimination: the element of moisture produces the inner and outer water realm, the element of heat produces the inner and outer fire realm, the element of motion produces the inner and outer wind realm, and the element of segmentation produces the inner and outer earth realm; apart from space, through clinging to perverse truths, the five aggregates gather and the forms produced by the great elements arise. Mahāmati, as for consciousness, because it arises with clinging to the sphere of various words as its cause, it continues to receive birth in other destinies. Mahāmati, forms produced by earth and the rest have the great elements as their cause, but it is not that the four great elements are the cause of the great elements. And why? Because whatever dharma has form and mark is made, not formless. Mahāmati, this mark of forms produced by the great elements is the discrimination of the sectarians; it is not what I teach.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, I shall now teach the essential marks of the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Mahāmati, form means the four great elements and the forms they produce, and these have distinct marks. Feeling and the rest are not form. Mahāmati, the immaterial aggregates are like space and have no number of four. Mahāmati, just as space transcends the marks of number, and yet one discriminates and says, ‘this is space,’ so too the immaterial aggregates transcend the marks of number, because they are beyond the four propositions of being and non-being and the rest. The marks of number are spoken of by the foolish, not by the noble ones; the noble ones say only that they are like an illusion and a magical creation, merely provisional designations beyond unity and difference, like a dream, like a reflection, without anything that exists. Because they do not understand the sphere traversed by noble wisdom, they see the aggregates and discrimination manifests before them; this is called the mark of the self-nature of the aggregates. Mahāmati, you should abandon such discrimination; having abandoned it, teach the dharma of stillness, cut off the sectarian views of all lands, purify the selflessness of dharmas, enter the ground of far-going, accomplish immeasurable sovereign samādhis, attain the mind-made body, and be fully endowed with the powers, transcendent faculties, and sovereignty of the samādhi of illusion, benefiting all beings like the great earth.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is of four kinds. What are the four? They are: the nirvāṇa of the non-existence of the self-nature of dharmas, the nirvāṇa of the non-existence of the nature of various marks, the nirvāṇa of the non-existence of the nature of the perceived self-nature, and the nirvāṇa of cutting off the stream of the self-nature and shared nature of the aggregates. Mahāmati, these four nirvāṇas are the doctrine of the sectarians; they are not what I teach. Mahāmati, what I teach is that the cessation of the discriminating ālaya-consciousness is called nirvāṇa.”
Mahāmati said: “World-Honored One, do you not establish eight kinds of consciousness?”
The Buddha said: “I do establish them.”
Mahāmati said: “If you establish them, why do you speak only of the cessation of the mental consciousness and not of the cessation of the seven consciousnesses?”

The Buddha said: “Mahāmati, because that is their cause and their condition, the seven consciousnesses come to be. Mahāmati, when the mental consciousness, discriminating objects, gives rise to clinging, it produces various habit-energies that nourish the storehouse consciousness; and because the manas, associated with it, follows along in its reckoning of self and what belongs to self, without a separate essence or mark, and because the storehouse consciousness is its cause and condition, it clings to the objects manifested by its own mind, and the cluster of mind arises and turns about as cause and effect. Mahāmati, just as the waves of the ocean are what is manifested by one’s own mind and rise and cease under the wind of objects, so when the mental consciousness ceases, the seven consciousnesses cease as well.”
Then the World-Honored One again spoke in verse:
“I do not, by self-nature, nor by the marks of making,
Teach the cessation of the consciousness that discriminates objects; thus I speak of nirvāṇa.
The mental consciousness is the cause of mind, and mind is the object of the manas;
Because of cause and condition, the consciousnesses arise in dependence.
As when a great torrent is exhausted, the waves no longer rise;
So when the mental consciousness ceases, the various consciousnesses do not arise.

“Moreover, Mahāmati, I shall now teach the marks of the differences of the imagined nature, so that you and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas may well understand this meaning, transcend all false imaginings and realize the realm of noble wisdom, know the doctrines of the sectarians, be far removed from the discrimination of grasper and grasped, and no longer grasp at the imagined marks amid the various marks of the dependent arising. Mahāmati, what are the marks of the differences of the imagined nature? They are: the discrimination of words, the discrimination of what is spoken, the discrimination of marks, the discrimination of wealth, the discrimination of self-nature, the discrimination of cause, the discrimination of views, the discrimination of principle, the discrimination of birth, the discrimination of non-birth, the discrimination of relation, and the discrimination of bondage and liberation. Mahāmati, these are the marks of the differences of the imagined nature. What is the discrimination of words? It is clinging to various beautiful sounds and phrases; this is called the discrimination of words. What is the discrimination of what is spoken? It is clinging to what is spoken as the realm realized by noble wisdom, and speaking in dependence on that; this is called the discrimination of what is spoken. What is the discrimination of marks? It is that, in regard to the things spoken of, like a thirsty beast’s notion, one discriminates and clings to all the marks of solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, and the rest; this is called the discrimination of marks. What is the discrimination of wealth? It is grasping at and clinging to various treasures of gold, silver, and the rest, and speaking of them; this is called the discrimination of wealth. What is the discrimination of self-nature? It is that, by evil views, one discriminates that this is the self-nature and definitely nothing else; this is called the discrimination of self-nature. What is the discrimination of cause? It is to discriminate causes and conditions as existent or non-existent, because by this mark of cause something is produced; this is called the discrimination of cause. What is the discrimination of views? It is the evil views of the sectarians, their clinging to being and non-being, unity and difference, both and neither, and the rest; this is called the discrimination of views. What is the discrimination of principle? It is to cling to the marks of self and what belongs to self and to speak of them; this is called the discrimination of principle. What is the discrimination of birth? It is to reckon that dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, arise from conditions; this is called the discrimination of birth. What is the discrimination of non-birth? It is to reckon that all dharmas are primordially unarisen, that before any conditions exist their essence already exists and does not arise from a cause; this is called the discrimination of non-birth. What is the discrimination of relation? It is that this and that are mutually connected, like a needle and thread; this is called the discrimination of relation. What is the discrimination of bondage and liberation? It is to cling to a cause that binds and to something bound, as when a person by the force of skillful means ties a rope and then unties it; this is called the discrimination of bondage and liberation. Mahāmati, these are the marks of the differences of the imagined nature, in which all the foolish and unenlightened cling to existence and non-existence. Mahāmati, in the midst of dependent arising they cling to the various imagined self-natures, as one who relies on an illusion sees various things, and the foolish, discriminating, see them as different from the illusion. Mahāmati, the illusion and the various things are neither different nor not different. If they were different, the illusion could not be the cause of the various things; if they were one, the illusion and the various things should have no difference, yet difference is seen; therefore they are neither different nor not different. Mahāmati, you and the bodhisattva mahāsattvas should not give rise to clinging regarding the existence or non-existence of the illusion.”
“The mind is bound by objects, and perception, thought, and wisdom follow along;
In the supreme place without marks, the wisdom of equality arises.
In the imagined it exists, but in dependent arising it does not;
The imagined is deluded grasping, while dependent arising is free from discrimination.
The various branches and parts that arise are like an illusion and are not accomplished;
Though various marks appear, in false discrimination there is nothing.
Those marks are themselves the fault, and all arise from the bondage of mind;
Those who vainly reckon do not understand the dharmas of dependent arising.
All these imagined natures are themselves dependent arising;
The imagined has various kinds, discriminated within dependent arising.
The conventional and the supreme meaning, and a third, arising without cause;
The imagined is the conventional, and when it is cut off, that is the noble realm.
As when a cultivator of contemplation sees various things appear;
In that there is no variety; so too are the marks of the imagined.
As with various cataracts of the eye, false imagining sees many forms;
Those forms are neither form nor formless; the unwise do not understand dependent arising.
As gold is free from dust and grime, as water is free from mud and turbidity;
As space is without clouds, so is false imagining purified.
There is no imagined nature, and yet there is dependent arising;
Assertion and denial are both ruined by discrimination.
If there were no imagined nature, and yet there were dependent arising;
Then a dharma without a dharma would exist, and a dharma would arise from nothing.
Relying on the cause of the imagined, dependent arising comes to be;
Mark and name ever follow one another, and from them the imagined is born.
Because dependent arising relies on the imagined, it is ultimately not accomplished;
Then purity is manifested, and this is called the supreme meaning.
The imagined has twelve kinds, and dependent arising has six;
The realm of suchness realized within oneself has no such differences there.
